one_liner: Scala macro-generated JSON codecs; decoding straight into case classes edged out RapidJSON's DOM (0.147 vs 0.154 s) in kostya/benchmarks.
what_it_does: A Scala library (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native) whose one-line `JsonCodecMaker.make` generates a JsonValueCodec[T] at compile time for case classes, ADTs, collections, java.time and similar types. You then call readFromArray/readFromStream/readFromByteBuffer/readFromString or the matching writeTo* functions to map JSON directly to and from typed Scala values. It has no DOM, AST or untyped document API, so its interface differs from RapidJSON's Document/Value model, but it can stream huge top-level arrays or whitespace-separated values through a callback (scanJsonArrayFromStream, scanJsonValuesFromStream).
how_it_is_fast: Black-box macros emit a specialized parser per type that reads UTF-8 bytes straight into constructor arguments, with no reflection, intermediate AST or hash maps. Keys go into a reused char buffer and are matched by sequential compares (up to 8 fields and 64 name chars) or by a @switch on a precomputed hash, and unknown fields are skipped by bracket/quote counting. Hot paths use SWAR word tricks through VarHandle byte-array views: 4-byte string scanning from borer, and 8-byte digit, java.time and UUID parsing from FastDoubleParser and simdjson ideas. Doubles take an exact pow10 fast path, then rust-lexical's 'moderate path' (multiplyHigh by precomputed power-of-10 mantissas), with Double.parseDouble only for near-halfway cases; output uses Schubfach/XJB shortest-double and James Anhalt integer printing, with parsers and writers pooled per thread in a ThreadLocal.
when_to_use: Scala services on the JVM that decode and encode known schemas (case classes, sealed-trait ADTs, Option, collections) from byte arrays or streams, for example HTTP bodies via its tapir, sttp, http4s, pekko-http or zio-http integrations.

Large documents where you only need some fields. Unmapped fields are skipped without being materialized: in the benchmark the RSS increase was 25.62 MiB vs RapidJSON DOM's 123.44 MiB for 524,288 records.
Multi-GB top-level JSON arrays or NDJSON-like value streams, processed one element at a time with scanJsonArrayFromStream or scanJsonValuesFromStream without holding the whole input in memory.

Untrusted input where you want safe defaults: fail-fast validation, stack-less exceptions, BigDecimal/BigInt capped at 308 digits, map/set insert caps, recursive types disabled, and only a fixed set of classes instantiated.

Number-heavy payloads that need correctly rounded double parsing and shortest round-trip double output, or as a faster parse/serialize backend for existing circe or play-json code through the booster modules.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ code, which is where RapidJSON lives. On the same benchmark page, simdjson On-Demand (0.060 s), gason (0.127 s), yyjson (0.131 s) and Mir asdf (0.133 s) all beat it, and it uses more memory and energy than RapidJSON g++.
Schema-less or dynamic JSON that you need to query as a tree. The library has no AST of its own, so you need circe, dijon or play-json on top.

Short-lived CLI or cold-start serverless processes. Base RSS was 283.94 MiB vs 113.21 MiB for RapidJSON, energy was 7.89 J vs 6.61 J, and neither JVM startup nor full JIT warm-up is part of the measured result.

Payloads dominated by long ASCII strings, or where most of the input is skipped. The author reports that simdjson-java (JDK Vector API) beats it on long strings and on skipping (issue #650). It uses SWAR, not explicit SIMD.
Recursive or cyclic object graphs (only acyclic graphs; recursive types need an opt-in flag), and Scala 3 union types or complex opaque types, which need hand-written custom codecs.

integration.form: module (Maven Central jars: jsoniter-scala-core at runtime; jsoniter-scala-macros as a compile-internal/provided dependency)
integration.dependencies: Runtime: scala-library only on the JVM, plus scala-java-time on Scala.js and Scala Native. Macros are compile-time only. Optional: jsoniter-scala-circe (needs circe-core).
integration.min_toolchain: Scala 2.12, 2.13 or 3.3 LTS+; JDK 11+ (v2.13.5.2 was the last release for JDK 8); Scala.js 1.0+; Scala Native 0.5+
integration.platforms: Any JVM on JDK 11+ (architecture-independent bytecode), GraalVM native-image, Scala.js (browsers/Node; WASM builds are benchmarked), Scala Native 0.5+
integration.thread_safety: The top-level read*/write* functions draw a JsonReader/JsonWriter from a per-thread ThreadLocal pool, so calls from different threads do not share parser state. They are non-reentrant within one thread, so nested calls must use the *Reentrant variants. Thread safety of the codec objects themselves is not documented.

gotchas: Nesting read/write calls on the same thread corrupts state because of the pooled reader/writer. For example, calling readFromString inside a scanJsonValuesFromStream callback breaks (README known issue 5, #923). Use the *Reentrant functions for all but the innermost call.

Unknown fields are skipped leniently by default. skip() only balances brackets and quotes and scans number-ish characters, so malformed JSON inside ignored fields can be accepted. Set skipUnexpectedFields=false to reject unknown fields instead of skipping them.

The safe defaults reject some valid data. A Map or Set with more than 1024 entries fails with 'too many map inserts'/'too many set inserts', and BigDecimal/BigInt values with 308+ digits fail, until you raise them via CodecMakerConfig. Duplicate keys throw, serializing null throws NPE, and total input length is not limited, so check it yourself (known issue 1).

The make() config is evaluated at compile time. It cannot depend on code in the same compilation module, and having two jsoniter-scala versions on the classpath gives 'Cannot evaluate a parameter of the make macro' errors. ADTs nested inside classes or functions can crash the compiler (#551), and escaped characters are not accepted inside numeric or java.time string values.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only JVM/Scala entry in this category, so choose it whenever the code is Scala: nothing else here runs there. In C/C++, glaze is the closest analogue (compile-time typed struct mapping), and simdjson, yyjson or gason are faster than jsoniter-scala on the same kostya page.
verified_claims_summary: In kostya/benchmarks' Json test (README update 2026-07-19, Xeon E-2324G, Debian Docker image), jsoniter-scala 2.39.1 was compiled with plain scalac 3.8.4 and run via the `scala` launcher (the README lists Java 24.0.2). It parsed the 524,288-record file and averaged x/y/z in 0.147 s. RapidJSON's DOM took 0.154 s with g++ 16.1.0 and 0.194 s with clang++ 22.1.8/libc++, both built with -O3 -march=native -flto: about 1.05x and 1.32x. The comparison is not like-for-like. jsoniter-scala decodes only x/y/z into case classes and skips the rest, while RapidJSON builds a full DOM with its default, less precise number parsing (RapidJSON Precise took 0.212/0.262 s). The JVM was warmed only by two tiny self-test documents.
status_note: Actively maintained: v2.41.1 was released 2026-09-25, while the benchmark pinned 2.39.1. It is MIT-licensed, depended on by tapir, sttp, caliban and smithy4s, and patch versions are binary-compatible both ways (minor versions backward only, checked with MiMa).
